tldr: MemOS is a memory operating system for large language models that treats memory as a first-class, schedulable resource, unifying parametric, activation, and plaintext memory through a standardized abstraction called MemCube to enable structured lifecycle management, cross-type transformation, and governance.
contributions: Introducing MemOS, a memory-centric execution framework that elevates memory to a first-class operational resource in LLMs
Proposing MemCube, a standardized memory abstraction with structured metadata and semantic payload that unifies heterogeneous memory types (parametric, activation, plaintext)

Designing a three-layer architecture (Interface, Operation, Infrastructure) supporting full memory lifecycle management including scheduling, version control, access governance, and cross-type transformation
Establishing transformation pathways between memory types—Plaintext to Activation, Plaintext/Activation to Parametric, and Parametric to Plaintext—for continuous memory evolution
methods: The authors propose a conceptual framework and prototype system design for MemOS. They classify memory into three types: parametric memory (knowledge in model weights), activation memory (transient inference states like KV-caches and attention weights), and plaintext memory (explicit external knowledge such as documents and knowledge graphs). A standardized Memory Cube (MemCube) unit encapsulates each memory type with descriptive metadata, governance attributes, behavioral indicators, and semantic payload. The architecture is organized into three layers—an Interface Layer with Memory APIs and pipeline operation chains, an Operation Layer with MemScheduler/MemLifecycle/MemOperator for scheduling and lifecycle management, and an Infrastructure Layer with MemVault/MemGovernance/MemStore for storage and cross-platform interoperability—forming a closed-loop memory I/O path.
results: The paper presents a design framework rather than empirical benchmark results; no quantitative performance numbers are reported. Key architectural capabilities described include: structured representation across three memory types, cross-type transformation pathways, version rollback and freezing for auditability, dynamic scheduling strategies (LRU, semantic similarity, label-based matching), and support for inter-agent collaboration via MemLoader/MemDumper for memory migration. The system enables traceable access via provenance logging, watermarking, access control, and compliance mechanisms. Future directions include cross-LLM memory sharing via a Memory Interchange Protocol (MIP), self-evolving MemBlocks, and a scalable decentralized memory marketplace.
limitations: The paper is a 'Short Version' presenting a conceptual framework and prototype system design without empirical evaluation or benchmark results
No quantitative validation is provided for the proposed architecture, scheduling strategies, or memory transformation pathways
The claimed benefits (reasoning coherence, adaptability, scalability) are asserted but not demonstrated through experiments
The system's practical overhead, scalability limits, and compatibility with existing LLM infrastructures are not addressed
